title: The pears (Confessions 2)
hook: young Augustine steals pears he doesn't want, just for the thrill

segments.voice: Yesterday, Monica's tears, and a bishop who told her the son of such tears could not be lost. Your line was the son of these tears. Who did you hold in mind? Day seven hundred thirty-four.

A pear tree, next to a vineyard. Loaded with fruit. And the pears, Augustine tells us, weren't even good: nothing special to look at, nothing special to eat. We step back a book now, to Book Two of the Confessions, when he's still a boy at home. Late one night, after hanging around the streets, he and a gang of friends go to that tree. They shake it. They haul off armloads of pears. They aren't hungry. They don't want pears. Long afterward, as he writes, this small theft is still bothering him.
screen: `A PEAR TREE BY A VINEYARD.` → `THE PEARS WEREN'T EVEN GOOD.` → `A GANG, LATE AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's what they did with the pears. They ate a few, Augustine says, and threw the rest to the pigs. He had better pears at home. So why? That's the whole question of the passage, and he won't let it go. He says the only pleasure in it was that it wasn't allowed. He loved, he says, not the pears, but the wrong itself. Then he goes looking for a motive the way a detective would. People who do terrible things, he says, usually want something: another man's wife, his land, money to live on, revenge. Even a cruel man has a reason. He can't find his. Then he finds one piece. He would not have done it alone. Alone, he says, it would have been no fun at all. It was the laughing together, the dare, the being in on it. He calls it a friendship that was no friend at all. Some readers hear an echo of another garden here, the tree in Genesis, fruit taken because it was forbidden. The loads were heavy, he says, but the stakes were nothing. Pears nobody wanted. Pig food. That's why it works. A big crime has big reasons. A pointless wrong shows the heart with nothing else in the way. And notice the tone. No list of punishments, no big drama. He's asking, in front of God, a question that's easy to skip: why did I do it?
screen: `NOT HUNGRY, NOT EVEN GOOD PEARS.` · `HE LOVED THE WRONG ITSELF.` · `ALONE, HE WOULDN'T HAVE DONE IT.` · `A SMALL WRONG SHOWS THE HEART.` · then, large: `WHY DID I DO IT?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look honestly at a pointless wrong. Settle, and breathe. Not your worst moment. A small one, with no good reason behind it. A cruel joke. Something broken for fun. A rumor passed on because it was juicy. Let it come up. Then ask Augustine's question, quietly: why did I do it? Who was I with? What did I want? Don't punish yourself. Just look. If you pray, you can name it to God, the way Augustine did. The bell holds the time.
The pears. A small theft from Augustine's boyhood, pears he didn't want, taken with friends for the thrill of the forbidden. Today's word.
Your line: why did I do it. Today, when you catch yourself doing something small and pointless, stop and ask the question. Day seven hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics prepare for confession with an examination of conscience, looking back over what they have done and why; Augustine's Confessions is read as an example of that kind of honest look.

what it means: Augustine uses it to ask why people do wrong they don't even want.
what a scholar hears: Confessions 2.4–9: a search for a motive that finds only the forbidden and the friends, and, for some readers, an echo of Eden's tree.
recall: one in being with the Father

notes: Confessions 2.4.9 paraphrased: pear tree near the vineyard, fruit tempting neither in color nor taste; a band of youths late at night after games in the streets; huge loads taken, a few eaten, the rest thrown to the pigs; better pears at home; pleasure in what was not allowed; loving the fault itself. Confirm.

2.5.10–11 paraphrased: every crime has a motive (Augustine's Catiline example is summarized, not named). 2.8.16–2.9.17 paraphrased: alone he would not have done it; 'friendship too unfriendly' rendered as 'a friendship that was no friend at all'. Confirm.
Hook says only 'long afterward' for the gap between the theft and the writing. Script avoids his age (the text gives his sixteenth year) to keep to the claims rule.
The Eden echo is attributed to 'some readers'. The match pair 'most of the haul' summarizes 'a few eaten, the rest thrown to the pigs'.

Audit pass: the teach said 'Augustine never says the theft was large. A few pears', which contradicts 2.4.9 (huge loads carried off) and the hook's 'armloads'; now 'the loads were heavy, but the stakes were nothing'. The motive list 'money, revenge, someone else's life' garbled 2.5.11 (another's wife or estate, a livelihood, revenge); corrected. Cut 'he's not beating himself up for show', which guessed at Augustine's motive.
